kegg-compound-txt.source_markdown:
This artifact is a TAB-delimited text file that can be used to color the **compound layer** of %(kegg-pathway-map)s files drawn by %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s.

The "compound layer" contains compound circles in maps. This file, passed to %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s with the `--compound-txt` option, can be paired with a %(kegg-reaction-txt)s file (`--reaction-txt`) to color the compound and reaction layers of a map at once.

## File format

The file must have a header line with a required `accession` column; the other columns are optional.

Each column name may appear only once, and names that start with `__` are reserved for anvi'o's own columns. Double quotes around a whole field or name, as R writes them, are dropped. Any other quote is kept as text, so a number that holds one is refused.

|Column|Required|Description|
|:--|:--|:--|
|`accession`|YES|A KEGG compound ID (`C#####`).|
|`sample`|NO|A sample of origin, enabling comparison across samples (and, with a %(groups-txt)s, across groups of samples). If this column is present, every row must have a sample.|
|*a value column*|NO|A SINGLE column with any name of your choosing, for coloring by a value instead of by presence/absence. Its values are numbers by default, for coloring by a continuous quantitative value. Its meaning is up to you (concentration, intensity, ...). With `--compound-value-type categorical`, its values are categorical values instead, such as `up` and `down` (see below). If this column is present, every row must have a value. This column is **auto-detected** as not being named `accession` or `sample`, and not being named by `--compound-border-column` or `--compound-bar-column`.|
|*a border column*|NO|A column whose values color the borders of compound circles on standard and overview maps. Each border is a ring just inside the black outline of a circle, and the value column still colors the fill. Global maps draw their circles without an outline, so they show no borders. The column can have any name. It is not auto-detected, so name it with `--compound-border-column`. Without that option, a file with a value column would have two candidate value columns and be refused. It cannot be `accession` or `sample`. Its values are numbers by default, and each must be a finite number. With `--compound-border-value-type categorical`, its values are categorical values instead. A row can leave its border cell empty, and then it has no border value. A border column with no values at all is refused. A file with a border column is read as text, so `NA` is a name in every column, including `sample`. With `--compound-color none`, a file without a value column or a bar column leaves its fills uncolored and colors only the rings of its circles. See %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s for the border options and their defaults.|
|*a bar column*|NO|A column of numbers that sets the size of a pie in each compound circle on standard and overview maps. The pie is a sector in the color of the fill, clockwise from 12 o'clock over a gray track, and the value column still colors the fill. Global maps do not show pies. The column can have any name. It is not auto-detected, so name it with `--compound-bar-column`. It cannot be `accession`, `sample`, or the border column. Each value must be a finite number of 0 or more, since a pie has no zero line from which to grow the other way. A row can leave its bar cell empty, and then it has no bar value. A bar column with no values at all is refused. A file with a bar column is read as text, as a file with a border column is. `--compound-color none` is refused with a bar column, since a pie takes the color of the fill. See the example below.|

To color by **presence** of accessions, do not include a value column. A border column is not a value column, so a file with a border column and no value column colors its fills by presence. On global and overview maps, these fills replace the colors that compounds would otherwise take from reactions. Global maps show no borders, so there such a file shows only presence. For such a file without a bar column, `--compound-color none` leaves the fills uncolored instead, so that the file colors only the rings of its circles. Compounds on global and overview maps then keep the colors that they take from a reaction layer. A circle on an overview map can then show the value of its reactions in its fill and the value of its compound in its ring. Without a reaction layer that colors fills, the circles are white inside their rings. A compound whose border cell is empty looks like a compound that is not in the file, and the run counts such rows. A bar column is not a value column either, so a file whose only column of values is its bar column colors its fills by presence, and its pies take those colors. On global and overview maps, the fills of such a file also replace the colors that compounds would otherwise take from reactions. Global maps draw these fills whole, without pies.

With a value column, a border column, or a bar column, no two rows may name the same accession in the same sample. Combine repeated measurements, or the separate ions of the same molecule, in whichever way suits your data.

A compound element on a map is defined by one or more KEGG compounds (~2%% of elements have multiple). Since a single compound circle can stand for several compounds, its color is the aggregate of whichever of its accessions are in the file (`--compound-accession-aggregation`; see below).

## Coloring by presence or quantitative values

The inclusion of different columns results in different coloring modes.

**No sample column, no value column**

Compounds are colored a single presence color, pink by default — set it with `--compound-color`, which takes a six-digit color hex code.

On global and overview maps, if reaction layer data supplied by %(kegg-reaction-txt)s is colored with `--original-color`, the compounds that those reactions touch are colored to match, just as they appear in the reference maps.

**Sample column, no value column**

Compounds are colored by sample (or, using a %(groups-txt)s, group) count or membership. Counts are drawn either in discrete bands, one per count (`--compound-sample-summary count`), or as a gradient from the lowest count to the highest (`--compound-sample-summary count_continuous`), the latter being the only one that works when there are more samples than the colormap has distinguishable colors — without `--compound-sample-summary`, discrete automatically switches to continuous given enough samples. By default, the scale stops at the highest count actually observed rather than at the number of samples, so that the colors spread over the counts that occur; use `--count-scale-max` to change the maximum value setting.

**Value column**

Compounds are colored by the continuous value through a sequential colormap (`--compound-colormap`, default `plasma_r`). The colorbar is labeled by the value column's header. A cyclic colormap called `clocktime` was defined in anvi'o to show a value column of clock times in hours. Give clock times `--compound-value-period 24`: each color scale of values then runs from 0 to 24 h and is colored by `clocktime`. Each reduction of the values takes their circular mean, `circular_mean`, so that 23.5 h and 0.5 h average to 0 h, not 12 h. See %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s.

A map element's constituent compound accessions are aggregated to a per-element value by `--compound-accession-aggregation` (`sum` by default) — this reduction happens within each sample.

With a `sample` column, `--draw-individual-files` and/or `--draw-grid` color maps of value column data that share a single `colorbar_compounds_samples.pdf` so that samples are comparable on the same scale. How the `unified` map, and with %(groups-txt)s the per-group maps, summarize samples is a separate choice (see below).

Each of these scales spans exactly the values it is given, which a few extreme elements can stretch until the rest cannot be told apart. `--compound-value-limits` bounds the `unified` map's scale and `--compound-individual-value-limits` the scale its per-sample or per-group maps share. These parameters take an argument of two values, a minimum and a maximum, either of which can be `none` to leave that end open while setting the other. A limit sets its end of the scale whether or not any value reaches it. The colorbar labels each limit. A limit that values lie past is marked `≤` or `≥`, since its color then stands for that value or anything past it.

A scale also sits wherever its own values leave it, which for a signed quantity means the neutral middle color of a diverging colormap lands somewhere other than zero. `--compound-value-center` and `--compound-individual-value-center` put a value at the middle of those two scales: used as a bare flag each centers its scale on 0, and each takes a number as an argument to center it on that instead. The scale is only ever widened to make room, running the same distance either side of the center and staying linear, so nothing is clipped that was not clipped already.

The two scales are colored by one colormap, `--compound-colormap`, unless `--compound-individual-colormap` gives the per-sample or per-group scale one of its own. That is worth doing where the two show quantities of different kinds: with `--compound-sample-summary std` the `unified` map shows how much samples disagree rather than how large their values are, so drawing it in the colors that show magnitude on the per-sample maps invites mistaking one scale for the other.

## Coloring by categorical values

A value column can hold **categorical values** instead of numbers. These are names, such as `up`, `down` and `same`, or the names of clusters. Give `--compound-value-type categorical` to read the column this way. Values written as numbers, such as `1` and `2`, are names too. A value is read as text, so `NA` is a value like any other. Every row needs a value. Each compound can have one value per sample, so repeated rows are refused, as they are for numbers.

Each value takes a color of its own. By default, the values take colors in sorted order. Where every value is a number, such as `-1`, `0` and `1`, the values are sorted as numbers. Otherwise the digits in the values are compared as numbers, so `cluster 2` comes before `cluster 10`. Up to 9 values take the colors of Matplotlib's `tab10` without its gray. The 10th to 18th values take the light colors of `tab20` without its light gray. Gray is left out because global maps draw the compounds they do not highlight in gray. To choose the colors yourself, give a %(kegg-value-colors-txt)s file with `--compound-value-colors`. The order of its rows is then the order of the values. More than 18 values need such a file, except in a grouped run without a sample rule, where no map shows the values. The legend lists the values in order, with the first value at the top.

**Choosing one value where several meet.** A circle on a map occasionally stands for more than one compound, and these can have different values. `--compound-accession-aggregation` then takes a rule that chooses one of them. Each compound gives one vote. The rules are `plurality_order` (the default), `plurality_random`, `plurality`, `majority`, `order` and `random`, as described in %(kegg-reaction-txt)s. `plurality` and `majority` can give no value. The circle is then left uncolored. The order of the values is the row order of the colors file, or else sorted order. A random choice comes from `--seed` (42 by default). `--compound-reverse-overlay` puts the last value on top where circles overlap.

**Samples.** With a `sample` column, the map of each sample shows that sample's values. Draw these maps with `--draw-individual-files` and/or `--draw-grid`. They share one legend, `colorbar_compounds_samples.pdf`. A value in one sample need not mean the same thing in another sample, so by default the `unified` map shows presence across the samples. It counts the samples that contain each element, however few samples there are. Coloring by which samples contain an element would use the `tab10` colors of the values. A color would then mean a sample on one map and a value on another. `--compound-sample-summary membership` still asks for it. Where a value does mean the same thing in every sample, give a rule to `--compound-sample-summary`. The rule then chooses one value per compound across the samples, and the `unified` map shows it.

**Groups of samples.** With a %(groups-txt)s, maps are drawn for groups rather than samples. By default, each group's map counts the group's samples, and the `unified` map counts the groups. Such a run colors nothing by the values, and anvi'o warns about it. A rule given to `--compound-sample-summary` chooses one value per element among the samples of each group. Each group's map then shows that value. A rule given to `--compound-group-summary` then chooses one value across the groups for the `unified` map. It needs a rule for the samples, since the groups otherwise have no values. Each sample with a value gives one vote in its group. Each group with a value gives one vote across the groups, whatever its size. With few voters, ties are common. With two groups, every disagreement between them is a tie, so `plurality_order` settles it by the order of the values. `majority` among the samples of a group shows a value only where more than half of the samples with a value agree. A sample without a value does not count, so one sample with a value is enough. Where the `unified` map counts the groups, `--group-threshold` decides when a group contains an element, as for any layer.

The options that shape a scale of numbers are refused for categorical values. These are the value limits and centers, `--compound-value-period`, `--compound-element-normalization` and `--compound-individual-colormap`. `--compound-colormap` colors only the presence on the `unified` map.

## Summarizing across samples and groups

There are three distinct reductions, each with its own option, plus one rescaling that is not a reduction. The first reduction applies whenever the file has a value column; everything below it needs a `sample` column:

|Level|Option|What it does|
|:--|:--|:--|
|accessions of a map element|`--compound-accession-aggregation` (an aggregation; `sum` by default; or a rule for categorical values)|the constituent accessions of a map element → that element's value|
|across samples|`--compound-sample-summary` (`count`, `count_continuous`, `membership`, an aggregation, or a rule for categorical values)|a set of samples → one value or one presence value per map element|
|across groups|`--compound-group-summary` (`count`, `count_continuous`, `membership`, an aggregation, or a rule for categorical values)|the groups of a %(groups-txt)s → one value or one presence value per map element|
|each sample's or group's value for an element|`--compound-element-normalization` (a normalization; none by default)|an element's value in one sample or group → that value rescaled against the element's values across all samples or groups|

An **aggregation** is `sum` (default), `mean`, `max`, `min`, `median`, `std` — or any other unsuggested pandas aggregation that reduces a series of numbers to one number, such as `var` or `sem`. Names that transform rather than reduce (`cumsum`) or that only a grouping offers (`first`) are rejected. Where an aggregation is undefined for the values available, as `std` is for a single value, the affected elements are left uncolored. `circular_mean` averages values that repeat after a period, such as clock times, and requires `--compound-value-period`. `angular_deviation` measures how far such values are spread apart, on the `unified` map only.

A summary pools the values of a **map element**, not of an accession. An element's value in a sample is the aggregate of its accessions in that sample. Without `--compound-element-normalization`, this is the value that the sample's own map draws, so the sample summary pools what the maps of the individual samples show. With groups, the group summary then pools the values of the groups.

The sample summary drives the `unified` map when there are no groups, and each per-group map (produced when using `--draw-individual-files` or `--draw-grid`) when there are. The group summary drives the `unified` map when there are groups.

Note that with groups, the per-group map either shows the count of that group's sample — the default case — or, with a `--compound-sample-summary` aggregation argument, the samples' pooled value; `--compound-sample-summary` is therefore not permitted with a presence name (`count`, `count_continuous` or `membership`) when using groups. For categorical values, a rule given to `--compound-sample-summary` colors each group's map by the value that it chooses among the group's samples.

The sample and group summaries in the `unified` maps both default to **presence**, even with a quantitative value column. The default is `membership` for 3 or fewer samples or groups. Above that, it is `count`. Where there are more samples or groups than the colormap has distinguishable colors, it is `count_continuous`. Presence is the default because it is meaningful across any set of samples. Pooling values is only meaningful across commensurable samples. For example, it makes sense to average metabolite concentrations across samples from replicate conditions, but not from unrelated conditions. Pooling values across samples is triggered by providing an aggregation argument to `--compound-sample-summary` or `--compound-group-summary`. `std` at this level maps how much samples disagree. A layer of categorical values counts the samples by default, however few there are.

A layer can show **presence in the overview and values per sample or group**. With the default presence summary, the `unified` map gets a colorbar of sample or group counts or memberships, while per-sample maps keep a continuous colorbar. The sample and group levels can be treated independently — replicate samples can be averaged within each condition (group) while the `unified` map summarizing all conditions shows in how many conditions each compound occurs, with a group containing a compound when at least half of its samples do:

{{ codestart }}
anvi-draw-kegg-pathways --compound-txt kegg-compound.txt \
                        --groups-txt %(groups-txt)s \
                        --group-threshold 0.5 \
                        --compound-sample-summary mean \
                        --compound-group-summary count \
                        --draw-individual-files \
                        -o output_dir
{{ codestop }}

## Normalizing an element across samples

With a `sample` column and a value column, each compound element in a sample map is colored by value aggregated across accessions in the element. `--compound-element-normalization` instead colors each element relative to all of the samples. Each element is rescaled against its own values across the samples, so under `relative_to_mean` a value of +0.25 means the sample has 25%% more of that element than it averages across samples, and -0.31 means 31%% less.

This cannot be worked out in the file itself before analyzing the maps, since each element in each map is related to one or more accessions — the same accession factors into different rescaled element values on each map.

anvi'o encodes a number of normalizations with names recognized as an argument: `relative_to_mean`, `relative_to_median`, `difference_from_mean`, `difference_from_median`, `log2_ratio_to_mean`, `log2_ratio_to_median`, `z_score`, `rank`, `fraction_of_max`, and `fraction_of_total`. With `--compound-value-period`, the only normalization is `difference_from_circular_mean`, the signed offset from the element's circular mean. A different name is taken to be a pandas Series method that transforms each value into a new value, such as `abs`.

Only the maps of individual samples or groups are rescaled, so element normalization needs `--draw-individual-files` and/or `--draw-grid`. The `unified` map summarizes the unnormalized values, so is unaffected by normalization.

{{ codestart }}
anvi-draw-kegg-pathways --compound-txt kegg-compound.txt \
                        --compound-element-normalization relative_to_mean \
                        --draw-individual-files \
                        -o output_dir
{{ codestop }}

## Maps with compounds that aren't colored

A small number of maps (`00121`, `00621`, `01052`, `01054`) contain compounds drawn as rectangles rather than circles. The rectangles overlay chemical structures on the base maps, so anvi'o does not color them in order to leave the structures unobscured.

## Examples

### Metabolomics (quantitative)

Color compound circles by measured concentrations. The `concentration` column is auto-detected as the value column.

|accession|concentration|
|:--|:--|
|C00031|55.0|
|C00092|12.0|
|C00074|30.5|

{{ codestart }}
anvi-draw-kegg-pathways --compound-txt kegg-compound.txt \
                        -o output_dir
{{ codestop }}

### Compound presence (single color)

With no value column and no `sample` column, present compounds are drawn one color.

|accession|
|:--|
|C00031|
|C00092|
|C00074|

{{ codestart }}
anvi-draw-kegg-pathways --compound-txt kegg-compound.txt \
                        -o output_dir
{{ codestop }}

### Comparing samples

Add a `sample` column to compare metabolomes (or other origins) on the same maps. Each sample's map is colored by its own values, while `--compound-sample-summary`/`--compound-group-summary` choose whether the summary views show presence or pooled values. See %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s for the full set of sample, group, and colormap options.

|accession|sample|concentration|
|:--|:--|:--|
|C00031|metabolome_A|55.0|
|C00031|metabolome_B|31.0|
|C00074|metabolome_A|30.5|

### With a reaction layer

Pair this file with a %(kegg-reaction-txt)s file to color both layers on the same maps, each by its own mode. For example, quantitative metabolomics of compounds can be shown alongside the presence of KOs in a genome.

{{ codestart }}
anvi-draw-kegg-pathways --reaction-txt %(kegg-reaction-txt)s \
                        --compound-txt kegg-compound.txt \
                        -o output_dir
{{ codestop }}

### Compound rings over reaction colors

On global and overview maps, compounds take their colors from the reactions that touch them. A compound file with only a border column keeps these colors with `--compound-color none`, and on overview maps it adds a ring to the circle of each of its compounds. Here the fills of the circles show the values of the reaction layer, and their rings show measured concentrations.

|accession|concentration|
|:--|:--|
|C00074|30.5|
|C00267|14.0|

{{ codestart }}
anvi-draw-kegg-pathways --reaction-txt %(kegg-reaction-txt)s \
                        --compound-txt kegg-compound.txt \
                        --compound-border-column concentration \
                        --compound-color none \
                        --pathway-numbers 01200 \
                        -o output_dir
{{ codestop }}

### Concentrations with detection pies (quantitative fill, pies of a second column)

Color the fill of each compound circle by concentration, and set the size of a pie in it by the percentage of replicates in which the compound was detected. `concentration` is auto-detected as the value column. `detected` is named as the bar column. The last row leaves its detection empty, so C00074 has no bar value in metabolome_B.

|accession|sample|concentration|detected|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|C00031|metabolome_A|55.0|100|
|C00031|metabolome_B|31.0|75|
|C00074|metabolome_A|30.5|50|
|C00074|metabolome_B|12.0||

{{ codestart }}
anvi-draw-kegg-pathways --compound-txt kegg-compound.txt \
                        --compound-bar-column detected \
                        --compound-bar-sample-summary mean \
                        --compound-bar-value-limits 0 100 \
                        --compound-bar-individual-value-limits 0 100 \
                        --draw-individual-files \
                        -o output_dir
{{ codestop }}

The map of each sample shows that sample's concentration in the color of each circle, and its detection in the size of the pie in the circle. A pie grows clockwise from 12 o'clock, which stands for 0. A circle with a fill and no bar value is left uncolored on a map that shows pies, so C00074 is uncolored on the standard and overview maps of metabolome_B. The bar summaries have no default, so the `unified` map shows pies here only because `--compound-bar-sample-summary` gives an aggregation. Its fills show presence across the samples, as they do by default. The bar accession aggregation defaults to `mean`, rather than `sum`. The limits make a full pie stand for 100%% on every map. Without them, each scale of pies would run from 0 to its largest value, and a full pie on the `unified` map would stand for 87.5, the mean detection of C00031. Pies are drawn in the circles of standard and overview maps, while global maps draw their circles keep whole fills. The keys of the pies are `bar_key_compounds.pdf` and `bar_key_compounds_samples.pdf`. See %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s for the options of pies and the maps that show them.
kegg-compound-txt.name: KEGG COMPOUND TXT

kegg-membership-colors-txt.source_markdown:
This artifact is a TAB-delimited text file that gives a color of your choosing to each sample, contigs database, genome, or group compared on %(kegg-pathway-map)s files drawn by %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s. A layer given this file is colored by membership.

A run compares each sample of a %(kegg-reaction-txt)s or %(kegg-compound-txt)s file, each %(contigs-db)s, or each genome of a %(pan-db)s. When a %(groups-txt)s groups any of these, the run compares each group. Normally anvi'o picks their colors for you by sampling a colormap (`--reaction-colormap`). This file says exactly which color each one gets instead. A color then means the same thing across every figure in a paper.

Pass it with `--reaction-membership-colors` for the reaction layer, and `--compound-membership-colors` for the compound layer of a %(kegg-compound-txt)s file. The two layers are colored independently, so each can take its own file; pointing both options at a single file gives them one set of colors and so one legend.

## File format

|Column|Required|Description|
|:--|:--|:--|
|*a name column*|YES|The **first** column, which can be headed anything you like, such as `sample`, `genome`, or `group`, so one file can describe samples in one run and groups in another without renaming the column. Each row names one sample, contigs database, genome, or group. A row can also name a combination of them (see below).|
|`color`|YES|A six-digit color hex code, such as `#1f77b4`. Color *names* are not accepted, since the colors that pathway maps reserve for their own unhighlighted elements are compared as hex codes.|

Here is an example file:

|sample|color|
|:--|:--|
|SAMPLE_1|#1f77b4|
|SAMPLE_2|#ff7f0e|
|SAMPLE_3|#2ca02c|

Each sample, contigs database, genome, or group that the run compares needs a color. Anvi'o will not fill in the gaps from a colormap, since that would put colors you chose and colors chosen for you on one scale. Names in the file that the run does *not* compare are reported and ignored, so one file can serve several runs that each draw a different subset.

## Coloring combinations

Coloring by membership colors a map element by exactly **which** samples, contigs databases, genomes, or groups contain it, so it needs a color for every *combination* of them. With three samples, that is seven colors rather than three.

A sample, contigs database, genome, or group on its own takes its own color. A combination takes the **blend** of its members' colors, mixed perceptually, so an element in the green sample and the blue sample is drawn in the color between them. To set a combination's color yourself, add a row that names its members separated by commas, exactly as the colorbar labels it:

|sample|color|
|:--|:--|
|SAMPLE_1|#1f77b4|
|SAMPLE_2|#ff7f0e|
|SAMPLE_3|#2ca02c|
|SAMPLE_1, SAMPLE_2|#7d5ba6|

Because a combination is written this way, no sample, contigs database, genome, or group may have a comma in its name.

Two combinations can of course blend to the same color, and a discrete colorbar labels one band per combination — so anvi'o refuses to draw a scale whose bands cannot be told apart, and reports how many distinct colors it got. Adding rows for the offending combinations fixes it. Note that no color scale distinguishes the combinations of more than a handful of samples, databases, genomes, or groups in any case. Past a few of them, color by count from a colormap instead. For contigs databases and pangenomes, use `--presence-colormap-scheme by_count`. For a text file, use a `count` sample or group summary, such as `--reaction-sample-summary count`. A run with a text file rejects `--presence-colormap-scheme`.

## Where the colors are used

**The 'unified' map and its colorbar.** Each combination takes its color as described above.

**Each sample's, database's, or genome's own map.** For a layer without a value column, `--draw-individual-files` and `--draw-grid` draw the map of each sample, contigs database, or genome in its own color rather than in one shared color, so a panel of a grid says which sample, database, or genome it shows. The panel's color also matches the band of that sample, database, or genome on the 'unified' map. (With `--skip-unified-maps` there is no 'unified' map and no band to match. Each panel is still drawn in its own color.)

**Each sample's map of a layer with a value column.** A value column of a %(kegg-reaction-txt)s or %(kegg-compound-txt)s file colors the map of each sample by that sample's values, not by the sample's color. Without a %(groups-txt)s, this file then colors only the 'unified' map. A layer of categorical values counts its samples on the 'unified' map by default, however few samples there are. With this file, that map shows which samples contain each element instead. Choose sample colors that differ from the colors of the values, since one color would otherwise mean a sample on the 'unified' map and a value on the map of a sample.

**Each group's own map, on request.** When a %(groups-txt)s groups the samples, databases, or genomes, a group's own map is colored by how many of the group's samples, databases, or genomes contain an element. That is a magnitude rather than an identity. The map takes its colors from `--group-colormap`. By default, this file does not change those colors. Giving `--group-colormap tint` instead builds each group's scale as a ramp. The ramp runs from a pale tint to the group's own color. Every group's ramp is built the same way, so the panels of a grid stay comparable, and the color of each panel shows which group it is.

{{ codestart }}
anvi-draw-kegg-pathways --reaction-txt %(kegg-reaction-txt)s \
                        --groups-txt %(groups-txt)s \
                        --group-threshold 0.5 \
                        --reaction-membership-colors %(kegg-membership-colors-txt)s \
                        --group-colormap tint \
                        --draw-grid \
                        -o OUTPUT_DIR
{{ codestop }}

The two decimal values that `--group-colormap` also accepts then say how far from white each ramp starts and stops, defaulting to 0.25 and 1.0. The pale end stops short of white on purpose: standard and overview maps keep white for their own unhighlighted elements, so a ramp reaching it could not be drawn there — anvi'o checks for this before writing any file and tells you to start the ramp further from white.

## When this file does not apply

This file gives a color to each sample, contigs database, genome, or group, so it needs a run that compares them. It also needs a layer colored by *which* of them contain an element.

- It cannot be combined with that layer's `--reaction-colormap`/`--compound-colormap`. A colormap is the other way to choose the layer's colors. It also cannot be combined with `--reaction-color`/`--compound-color` or `--original-color`. These color a layer without comparing samples, databases, genomes, or groups at all.
- It needs a `sample` column in a %(kegg-reaction-txt)s or %(kegg-compound-txt)s file, or more than one %(contigs-db)s, or a %(pan-db)s.
- It does not apply to coloring by *count* (`--presence-colormap-scheme by_count`, or a `count`/`count_continuous` sample or group summary). A count says how many samples, databases, genomes, or groups contain an element, not which ones, so a count has no single sample, database, genome, or group whose color it could take.
kegg-membership-colors-txt.name: KEGG MEMBERSHIP COLORS TXT

kegg-value-colors-txt.source_markdown:
This artifact is a TAB-delimited text file that gives a color of your choosing to each **categorical value** of a %(kegg-reaction-txt)s or %(kegg-compound-txt)s file drawn by %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s.

A value column holds categorical values when the run gives `--reaction-value-type categorical` or `--compound-value-type categorical`. Such values are names, such as `up`, `down` and `same`. Normally anvi'o gives them its default colors in sorted order. This file says exactly which color each value gets instead, so that a color means the same thing across every figure in a paper. It also sets the order of the values.

Pass it with `--reaction-value-colors` for the reaction layer, and `--compound-value-colors` for the compound layer. The two layers are colored independently, so each can take its own file.

A border column holds categorical values when the run gives `--reaction-border-value-type categorical` or `--compound-border-value-type categorical` (see %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s). Pass this file with `--reaction-border-value-colors` or `--compound-border-value-colors` to color the values of a border column. Without it, border values take 7 default colors of their own, those of Matplotlib's `Dark2` without its gray, in this order: `#d95f02`, `#7570b3`, `#e6ab02`, `#a6761d`, `#1b9e77`, `#e7298a`, and `#66a61e`. More than 7 border values need this file. Border colors are not checked against the colors that maps reserve, so black, white, and gray can color borders.

## File format

|Column|Required|Description|
|:--|:--|:--|
|*a value column*|YES|The **first** column, which can be headed anything you like, such as `value` or `status`. Each row names one categorical value.|
|`color`|YES|A six-digit color hex code, such as `#1f77b4`. Color *names* are not accepted, since the colors that pathway maps reserve for their own unhighlighted elements are compared as hex codes.|

Here is an example file:

|status|color|
|:--|:--|
|up|#d62728|
|down|#1f77b4|
|same|#bcbd22|

Every value of the layer needs a color. Anvi'o will not fill in the gaps with its default colors, since that would put colors you chose and colors chosen for you in one legend. Values in this file that the layer does *not* have are reported and ignored, so one file can serve several runs. Two values cannot share a color, since the maps and the legend could not tell them apart.

A value is a whole name, so a comma in it is just part of the name. This differs from a %(kegg-membership-colors-txt)s file, where a comma joins the names of a combination.

## The order of the rows

The order of the rows is the order of the values. It is used in three places.

- **The legend.** The legend lists the values in this order, with the first value at the top.
- **Drawing.** Where map elements overlap, the first value is drawn on top. `--reaction-reverse-overlay`/`--compound-reverse-overlay` puts the last value on top instead.
- **Choosing one value.** Where several values meet, a rule chooses one. `plurality_order` gives a tie to the value that comes first, and `order` always takes the value that comes first. If `up` is in an earlier row than `same`, `order` chooses `up` for a map element whose KOs have both.

For the values of a border column, the order is used only in the legend and in choosing one value. It does not set the order of drawing, which follows the fills of the elements.

## When this file does not apply

This file needs categorical values. It is refused unless the layer's value type is `categorical`. Given for a border column, it is refused unless `--reaction-border-value-type` or `--compound-border-value-type` is `categorical`.

With a %(groups-txt)s, a layer whose file has a `sample` column also needs a rule in its sample summary, or this file is refused. That is `--reaction-sample-summary` for the reaction layer and `--compound-sample-summary` for the compound layer. Without a rule, each group's map counts the group's samples. No map then shows the values, so they take no colors, and there can be more than 18 of them without this file. A layer whose file has no `sample` column shows the same values on every group's map, so this file is accepted for that layer without a rule.

The same holds for a border column, whose rule goes in `--reaction-border-sample-summary` or `--compound-border-sample-summary`. Without a rule, no map shows the borders.
kegg-value-colors-txt.name: KEGG VALUE COLORS TXT

kegg-slice-key-txt.source_markdown:
This artifact is a TAB-delimited text file written by %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s. It lists the slices of the reaction elements drawn on %(kegg-pathway-map)s files, or the slices of the rings that color their borders.

With `--reaction-slice-by`, a box or line that stands for several KOs, KEGG reactions, or genes is drawn in slices, one for each accession or gene with a value on the map. Slices are too narrow to label, and a box label names only the first KO of the element. This table says what each slice stands for. The program writes it as `slice_key_reactions.txt` at the top of the output directory, beside the colorbars. One file covers every map of the run. Options that arrange the map files, such as `--categorize-files` and `--collate-files-by-map`, do not move it. See %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s for how slices are drawn and how their shares are found.

With `--reaction-border-slice-by`, the ring that colors the border of a box is divided among the accessions or genes with border values. The program then writes a second table of the same form, `slice_key_reactions_border.txt`, beside the first. It lists the slices of the rings, as described in [Slices of rings](#slices-of-rings).

## File format

The file has a header line and these columns:

|Column|Description|
|:--|:--|
|`map`|The number of the KEGG map, such as `00010`.|
|`drawn_map`|Which map of that KEGG map was drawn. This is `unified` for the `unified` map, or the name of a sample or group for the map of that sample or group. The one map drawn from a %(kegg-reaction-txt)s without a `sample` column is `unified`.|
|`entry_id`|The ID of the element's entry in the map's KGML file.|
|`x`|The x coordinate of the element in the map's KGML file. For a box, this is its center. For a line, this is the point near the middle of its first piece where Biopython puts the label of a line.|
|`y`|The y coordinate of the same point.|
|`label`|The label of the element in the KGML file, such as `K01623...`.|
|`slice`|The position of the slice, counting from 1. The slices of a box count from the left. The slices of a line count from its first point in the KGML file, within each cycle of dashes. This is blank for an element drawn whole for a reason.|
|`accession`|The KO or KEGG reaction that the slice stands for. For a slice of a gene (`--reaction-slice-by gene`), this lists the gene's KOs or KEGG reactions in the element, in KGML order, joined by commas without spaces, such as `K01623,K01624`. These are the accessions of the element for which the gene has rows anywhere in the file, so a gene has the same label on every map. On a map where the gene has rows for only some of them, all are still listed.|
|`gene_id`|The gene that the slice stands for, with `--reaction-slice-by gene`. This is blank for a slice of an accession.|
|`value`|The value of the accession or gene on the drawn map. This is a number, or a categorical value with `--reaction-value-type categorical`. A gene with rows for two or more accessions of the element takes the mean of these rows in a sample by default. On the map of a group or the `unified` map, the value is the summary of the values in the samples or groups.|
|`share`|The share of the element's width or length that the slice takes. The shares of an element on a drawn map sum to 1.|
|`color`|The color of the slice, as a hex code. For an element drawn whole, it is the color of the whole element.|
|`drawn_whole`|Blank for a slice that is drawn. For an element drawn whole, it gives the reason, `over the cap` for a box or `line too short` for a line. A ring can also be drawn whole for the reason `fill not sliced`.|
|`bar`|Only in the table of a layer with a bar column (`--reaction-bar-column`). The bar value of the accession or gene on the drawn map, which its column of the box shows as a bar. A box drawn whole lists the bar values of the slices it would have had. The column is blank where the slice has no bar value, for the slices of lines, which take no bars, and on a map that shows no bars, such as the `unified` map without `--reaction-bar-sample-summary`. A column without a bar value is white in the default style, and keeps its color without a strip in the `strip` style.|

## Rows

Each row is one slice on one drawn map. An element on the `unified` map and on the maps of three samples has rows for each of the four maps. Its slices can differ from map to map, since an accession or gene gets a slice only on the maps where it has a value. The same position can then hold different accessions or genes on different maps.

An element with one slice is drawn whole in the color of that slice. It has one row, with `slice` 1 and `share` 1.0.

An element with more slices than fit is drawn whole in the color of a stand-in value. A box is drawn whole where a slice of equal width would be narrower than 8 points. In a layer with a border column, the slices of a box fit inside its ring, which leaves 85 of its 92 points. A line is drawn whole where any of its pieces would give a slice of equal length shorter than the line is wide. Only the part of the piece that compound circles leave visible counts. Such an element has a row for each slice it would have had. These rows have a blank `slice`, the share and value that each slice would have had, and the color of the whole element. `drawn_whole` gives the reason. The stand-in value itself is not listed.

Elements left uncolored have no rows. These include an element whose slices with values all have a weight of 0, and an element drawn whole whose stand-in value is undefined.

The rows are sorted by `map`, then by `drawn_map`, then by entry ID, and then by `slice`. The `unified` map comes first, and the maps of the samples or groups follow in the order in which they are drawn. Rows name maps, not files. A map drawn only as a panel of a grid is listed under its sample or group, like any other. The file is written whenever slicing is on. It holds only the header if no slice was drawn.

## Examples

Here are rows for one box of map `00010`, drawn in equal slices on the maps of two samples. The box has two slices on the map of `SAMPLE_1`. On the map of `SAMPLE_2`, only K16306 has a value, so it fills the box.

|map|drawn_map|entry_id|x|y|label|slice|accession|gene_id|value|share|color|drawn_whole|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|00010|SAMPLE_1|18|966|814|K01623...|1|K01622||36.5|0.5|#a01a9c||
|00010|SAMPLE_1|18|966|814|K01623...|2|K16306||15.5|0.5|#f79143||
|00010|SAMPLE_2|18|966|814|K01623...|1|K16306||30.5|1.0|#c13b82||

Here are rows for the same box from a run sliced by gene, on the maps of two other samples, `control` and `treated`. The rows come from the example file for slices of genes in %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s. `gene_1` has rows for K01623 and K01624, so it is one slice. On the map of `treated`, its rows are 1.2 for K01623 and 0.8 for K01624, so its value is their mean, 1.0. `gene_2` has a row for K01623 only.

|map|drawn_map|entry_id|x|y|label|slice|accession|gene_id|value|share|color|drawn_whole|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|00010|control|18|966|814|K01623...|1|K01623,K01624|gene_1|0.2|0.5|#db5c68||
|00010|control|18|966|814|K01623...|2|K01623|gene_2|0.5|0.5|#a31e9a||
|00010|treated|18|966|814|K01623...|1|K01623,K01624|gene_1|1.0|0.5|#0d0887||
|00010|treated|18|966|814|K01623...|2|K01623|gene_2|-0.4|0.5|#f0f921||

Here are the first three of the 14 rows of a box drawn whole, from a run without samples. The box would have had 14 slices, which is more than the 11 that fit. The whole box takes one color.

|map|drawn_map|entry_id|x|y|label|slice|accession|gene_id|value|share|color|drawn_whole|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|00190|unified|255|960|772|K00234...||K00234||16.5|0.09090909090909091|#c33d80|over the cap|
|00190|unified|255|960|772|K00234...||K00235||7.5|0.12121212121212122|#c33d80|over the cap|
|00190|unified|255|960|772|K00234...||K00236||21.5|0.030303030303030304|#c33d80|over the cap|

## Columns of bars

With `--reaction-bar-column`, the table of the layer has the column `bar` at the end. Each column of a box shows the bar of its own accession or gene, so the bar value belongs to the slice of its row. A box drawn whole shows one bar, the mean of the bar values of its slices, weighted by their shares, and that mean is not listed. Here are rows for the box of the first example from a file with `expression` as its value column and `coverage` as its bar column, on the `unified` map, where `--reaction-sample-summary mean` and `--reaction-bar-sample-summary mean` pool the samples.

|map|drawn_map|entry_id|x|y|label|slice|accession|gene_id|value|share|color|drawn_whole|bar|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...|1|K01623||6.0|0.25|#f79143||13.333333333333334|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...|2|K01624||7.666666666666667|0.25|#e56a5d||21.0|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...|3|K01622||16.0|0.25|#0d0887||17.25|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...|4|K16306||2.5|0.25|#f0f921||15.0|

A file whose only column of values is its bar column colors its fills by presence. Its bars are sliced on their own, among the accessions or genes with bar values, and its table lists these columns. Their `value` is blank, since the fill has none, and their `color` is the one color of the fill. Here are rows of the same box from such a file, with `coverage` as its bar column and no samples.

|map|drawn_map|entry_id|x|y|label|slice|accession|gene_id|value|share|color|drawn_whole|bar|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...|1|K01624|||0.3333333333333333|#2ca02c||33.5|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...|2|K01622|||0.3333333333333333|#2ca02c||36.5|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...|3|K16306|||0.3333333333333333|#2ca02c||23.0|

The tables of layers without a bar column, and the tables of rings, have no `bar` column.

## Slices of rings

The table of the slices of rings, `slice_key_reactions_border.txt`, has the same columns. `value` and `color` are those of the border column, and `drawn_whole` gives why a ring is drawn whole. The rings of a run are either aligned with the slices of the fill or divided on their own, and the positions and shares depend on which.

- **Aligned with the fill.** Where `--reaction-slice-by` and `--reaction-border-slice-by` name the same unit, and the file has a value column for the fill, each column of the fill takes the border value of its own accession or gene, as bands above and below it. A row lists such a column. Its `slice` and `share` are those of the column in `slice_key_reactions.txt`. A column without a border value has no row.
- **Divided on its own.** Otherwise, each ring is divided among its accessions or genes with border values. The slices count clockwise from the top left corner of the box, and `share` is the share of the ring that a slice takes.

A ring of one slice is drawn whole in the color of that slice, with `slice` 1 and `share` 1.0. Rings can also be drawn whole for these reasons, in the color of a stand-in value:

- `over the cap`. An aligned ring is drawn whole where its fill has more slices than fit. Its rows list the units with both a slice of the fill and a border value, with the shares of the fill. A ring divided on its own is drawn whole where it would have more than 11 slices.
- `fill not sliced`. An aligned ring is drawn whole where the fill of its box is not sliced, since the map shows presence or the box has no fill value there. Its rows list every unit with a border value, with equal shares.

Rings left out have no rows. These include a ring whose slices with values all have a weight of 0, and a ring drawn whole whose stand-in value is undefined.

Here are rows of the aligned rings of the box of the first example, on the map of `SAMPLE_1`. The fill was sliced by KO, with shares from a column of weights, and the border column holds the categorical values `up` and `down`.

|map|drawn_map|entry_id|x|y|label|slice|accession|gene_id|value|share|color|drawn_whole|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|00010|SAMPLE_1|18|966|814|K01623...|1|K01624||up|0.47619047619047616|#d62728||
|00010|SAMPLE_1|18|966|814|K01623...|2|K01622||down|0.047619047619047616|#1f77b4||
|00010|SAMPLE_1|18|966|814|K01623...|3|K16306||up|0.47619047619047616|#d62728||

Here are rows of the same box on the `unified` map of that run, where the fills show presence. The fill is not sliced, so the ring is whole. Its color is that of `up`, which `plurality_order` chooses among the three KOs.

|map|drawn_map|entry_id|x|y|label|slice|accession|gene_id|value|share|color|drawn_whole|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...||K01624||up|0.3333333333333333|#d62728|fill not sliced|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...||K01622||down|0.3333333333333333|#d62728|fill not sliced|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...||K16306||up|0.3333333333333333|#d62728|fill not sliced|

kegg-label-key-txt.source_markdown:
This artifact is a TAB-delimited text file written by %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s. It lists the reaction boxes drawn without their labels on %(kegg-pathway-map)s files, because of the bars inside them.

With `--reaction-bar-column`, a map whose bar scale has values on both sides of 0 draws bars that grow both ways from a gray zero line. The label of a box fills its upper half, where it would hide the zero line and the ends of short bars, so the boxes of the default `fill` style are drawn without their labels. A box whose bar runs up its height is drawn without its label too, since the top of its bar would run behind the label. Bars run up their boxes with `--reaction-bar-orientation vertical`, and by default in boxes sliced with `--reaction-slice-by` whose accessions or genes have two or more bar values. This table says what each of these boxes stands for. The program writes it as `label_key_reactions.txt` at the top of the output directory, beside the bar keys. One file covers every map of the run. It is written where the bars are vertical, or where the bar scale of the `unified` map, or the scale shared by the maps of the samples or groups, has values on both sides of 0. Boxes of the `strip` style keep their labels, so a run of strips writes no table. See %(anvi-draw-kegg-pathways)s for how bars are drawn.

## File format

The file has a header line and these columns:

|Column|Description|
|:--|:--|
|`map`|The number of the KEGG map, such as `00010`.|
|`drawn_map`|Which map of that KEGG map was drawn. This is `unified` for the `unified` map, or the name of a sample or group for the map of that sample or group. A %(kegg-reaction-txt)s without a `sample` column draws only the `unified` map, unless a %(kegg-compound-txt)s with a `sample` column draws maps of samples too. Its boxes are then the same on every map, and each map lists them.|
|`entry_id`|The ID of the box's entry in the map's KGML file.|
|`x`|The x coordinate of the center of the box in the map's KGML file.|
|`y`|The y coordinate of the center of the box.|
|`label`|The label of the box in the KGML file, such as `K01623...`. This is the label that was not drawn.|
|`accession`|The KOs or KEGG reactions of the box that the file has on the drawn map, in KGML order, joined by commas without spaces, such as `K01622,K16306`. On the map of a sample, these are the accessions with rows in that sample. On the map of a group or the `unified` map, they are those of any of its samples. A file without a `sample` column gives every map all of its accessions.|
|`bar`|The bar value of the box on the drawn map. On the map of a group or the `unified` map of a file with a `sample` column, it is the summary of the bar values in the samples or groups. It is blank for a box drawn in columns with `--reaction-slice-by`, whose bar values the %(kegg-slice-key-txt)s gives slice by slice. A sliced box drawn whole lists the one bar it shows, such as the mean of the bar values of its slices, weighted by their shares.|

## Rows

Each row is one box on one drawn map. The rows are sorted by `map`, then by `drawn_map`, then by entry ID. The `unified` map comes first, and the maps of the samples or groups follow in the order in which they are drawn. Rows name maps, not files. A map drawn only as a panel of a grid is listed under its sample or group, like any other.

A box is listed on a drawn map only where its bar is vertical or its bar scale has values on both sides of 0. The `unified` map and the maps of the samples or groups have bar scales of their own, so a box can be listed on one and labeled on the other. A box left uncolored for want of a bar value keeps its label and is not listed. Boxes are listed whether or not `--reaction-labels` labels standard maps.

## Examples

Here are rows for three boxes of map `00010`, from a file of log ratios in three samples, with `--reaction-bar-sample-summary mean`. The bar scale of the `unified` map runs from -1 to 3.5, and the scale shared by the maps of the samples from -1 to 5. On the `unified` map, the box of entry 18 shows the mean of its bar values across the samples. On the map of `SAMPLE_1`, only two of its KOs have rows.

|map|drawn_map|entry_id|x|y|label|accession|bar|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|00010|unified|18|966|814|K01623...|K01624,K01622,K16306|3.4166666666666665|
|00010|unified|61|916|968|K00134...|K00134|-0.5|
|00010|unified|159|1148|1592|K01007|K01007|-1.0|
|00010|SAMPLE_1|18|966|814|K01623...|K01622,K16306|2.75|
kegg-label-key-txt.name: KEGG LABEL KEY TXT

enzymes-list-for-module.source_markdown:
This is a 3-column, tab-delimited file that lists the enzymes to be included in a user-defined metabolic module. It is used as input to %(anvi-script-gen-user-module-file)s, which will create a module file using the enzyme definitions within the file.

The first column in this file must be an enzyme accession, the second column must be the annotation source of the enzyme, and the third column specifies the orthology (or functional definition) of the enzyme. Note that if the annotation source is 'KOfam' and the enzyme is a KEGG Ortholog that is present in the KEGG KOfam profiles in %(kegg-data)s, then the orthology field can be blank. In this case, the orthology field will be filled in automatically with the enzyme's known orthology in the KOfam data.

Here is an example file:

|**enzyme**|**source**|**orthology**|
|:--|:--|:--|
|K01657|KOfam||
|K01658|KOfam||
|PF06603.14|METABOLISM_HMM|UpxZ|
|COG1362|COG20_FUNCTION|Aspartyl aminopeptidase|
|TIGR01709.2|TIGRFAM|type II secretion system protein GspL|
enzymes-list-for-module.name: ENZYMES LIST

contig-rename-report-txt.source_markdown:
A two-column TAB-delmited file containing the association between an old set of names in a %(fasta)s file, and a new set of names.

In each line, the first column lists the *original name* and the second column lists the *new name* of any given contig.

By default, this file is generated by %(anvi-script-reformat-fasta)s, when it is run with the flags `--simplify-names` and `--report-file`.
contig-rename-report-txt.name: CONTIG RENAME REPORT TXT

where,

* `contig`: name of the reference sequence in the %(bam-file)s.
* `contig_length`: the actual length of the reference sequence.
* `status`: the classification result, and whether the contig determined to be 'circular', 'linear', or none ('indeterminate').
* `circularity_support`: a score that ranges from 0 to 1 and indicates the strenght of evidence that support circularity.
* `edge_coherence`: a score that ranges from 0 to 1 and indicates the fraction of edge-mapping reads whose mates also map to this contig.
* `num_fr_pairs`: number of `FR` (forward-reverse) pairs (these are the normal pairs that map like normal people do).
* `expected_rf_pairs`: the expected number of `RF` pairs *if* the contig were circular, calculated from `num_fr_pairs` and the geometry of insert size vs contig length.
* `observed_rf_pairs`: the total number of `RF`-oriented read pairs that are actually found on this contig.
* `supporting_rf_pairs`: the umber of `RF` pairs whose circular insert size fell within the expected insert size distribution (i.e., weird pairs that do look like plausible junction-spanning pairs).
* `num_edge_reads`: the number of reads mapping within 'average insert size' length of contig edges.
* `num_edge_reads_incoherent`: the number of edge reads whose mate maps to a different contig.
* `flags`: warning flags for edge cases.

metabolite-exchange-predictions.source_markdown:
This page describes the output files produced by the program %(anvi-predict-metabolic-exchanges)s. Breifly, the most important outputs of this program are:

- a file of 'potentially-exchanged compounds' (filename suffix: `-potentially-exchanged-compounds.txt`)
- a file of 'unique compounds' (filename suffix: `-unique-compounds.txt`)

If you ran the prediction method that uses KEGG Pathway Map walks to examine chains of reactions leading to the production reactions (or away from the consumption reactions) of a given compound, then you will get an additional output file:

- a file of evidence supporting the predictions of 'potentially-exchanged compounds' from Pathway Map walks

## Example output files

All of the examples shown here were generated by running %(anvi-predict-metabolic-exchanges)s on the genomes of _Baumannia cicadellinicola_ and _Sulcia muelleri_, which are known to exchange amino acids and vitamins as part of their co-symbiosis within the glassy-winged sharpshooter ([Wu et al, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0040188)).

### Potentially-exchanged compounds

Each line of this file describes a metabolite that is potentially exchanged between two organisms. For each prediction, it describes which genomes are involved, which organism is the predicted producer and consumer, and the prediction method. If the Pathway Walk prediction method was run, then the file will also contain a basic summary of the evidence supporting each prediction.

|**`compound_id`**|**`compound_name`**|**`genomes`**|**`produced_by`**|**`consumed_by`**|**`prediction_method`**|**`max_reaction_chain_length`**|**`max_production_chain_length`**|**`production_overlap_length`**|**`production_overlap_proportion`**|**`production_chain_pathway_map`**|**`max_consumption_chain_length`**|**`consumption_overlap_length`**|**`consumption_overlap_proportion`**|**`consumption_chain_pathway_map`**|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|cpd00024|2-Oxoglutarate|B_cica,S_muel|B_cica|S_muel|Pathway_Map_Walk|3|2|None|None|00340|1|1|1.0|00220|
|cpd00033|Glycine|B_cica,S_muel|B_cica|S_muel|Pathway_Map_Walk|2|1|None|None|00480|1|1|1.0|00630|
|cpd00039|L-Lysine|S_muel,B_cica|S_muel|B_cica|Pathway_Map_Walk|8|7|None|None|00300|1|1|1.0|00970|

Below are the column descriptions.

**Standard columns**
- `compound_id`: the ModelSEED ID of the potentially-exchanged compound
- `compound_name`: the human-readable name of the compound
- `genomes`: which genomes are involved in the potential exchange (labeled by the name set in the %(contigs-db)s)
- `produced_by`: which genome(s) encode enzymes for reactions that produce the compound
- `consumed_by`: which genome(s) encode enzymes for reactions that consume the compound
- `prediction_method`: how did we identify this exchange? By walking over KEGG Pathway Maps or by isolating metabolites in the merged reaction network?

**Supporting evidence columns**

These columns summarize the 'best' evidence we could find that this compound is potentially-exchanged from KEGG Pathway Map walks. By 'best', we mean that we report the longest production chain of reactions in the 'producer' organism and the longest consumption chain of reactions in the 'consumer'. Longer reaction chains indicate that the compound transfer is not isolated within either genome's reaction network; i.e., it is part of a more extensive chain of chemical transformations. When there are two reaction chains with the same maximum length, we report the one with the smallest (real number) proportion of overlap between the two genomes, and when _those_ values are also the same between two chains, we report the one with the smallest (real number) overlap length. If multiple Pathway Maps have chains of exactly the same length _and_ overlap proportion _and_ overlap length, then we report all of them. Note that a lot of these evidence columns can have `None` values in them, which means that the evidence did not apply to a particular case.

- `max_reaction_chain_length`: The total length of the longest production and consumption reaction chains (`max_production_chain_length` + `max_consumption_chain_length`)
- `max_production_chain_length`: The length of the longest production chain in the 'producer' organism
- `production_overlap_length`: If the 'consumer' organism has enzymes that belong to the Pathway Map containing the production chain, then how long is the overlap between the 'consumer' organism's production chains for the compound and the producer's production chain? If this is `None`, it means the 'consumer' didn't have any production chains for the compound and we couldn't compute an overlap.
- `production_overlap_proportion`: If there was overlap between the production chains in the producer and consumer, what proportion of reactions were found in both organisms?
- `production_chain_pathway_map`: The ID(s) of the KEGG Pathway Map in which we found the "best" production chain. If there are multiple Pathway Maps in a comma-separated list here, it means they all included a production chain with the same (maximum) length, (minimum) overlap proportion, and (minimum) overlap length.
- `max_consumption_chain_length`: The length of the longest consumption chain in the 'consumer' organism
- `consumption_overlap_length`: If the 'producer' organism has enzymes that belong to the Pathway Map containing the consumption chain, then how long is the overlap between the 'producer' organism's consumption chains for the compound and the consumer's production chain? If this is `None`, it means the 'producer' didn't have any consumption chains for the compound and we couldn't compute an overlap.
- `consumption_overlap_proportion`: If there was overlap between the consumption chains in the producer and consumer, what proportion of reactions were found in both organisms?
- `consumption_chain_pathway_map`: The ID(s) of the KEGG Pathway Map in which we found the "best" consumption chain. If there are multiple Pathway Maps in a comma-separated list here, it means they all included a consumption chain with the same (maximum) length, (minimum) overlap proportion, and (minimum) overlap length.

If you are curious about the other Pathway Walk evidence for a given prediction, take a look at the 'Evidence' file (described in the next section).

**Additional columns**

Some columns can be added by using particular flags.

- `equivalent_compound_id`: Shows the ModelSEED ID of any compound deemed equivalent to the reported `compound_id`. Added by running the program with either `--use-equivalent-amino-acids` or `--custom-equivalent-compounds-file`.
- `production_rxn_ids_*` and `consumption_rxn_ids_*`: The ModelSEED ID of any production/consumption reactions the compound participates in, specific to the reaction network of a given genome. Added by using the `--add-reactions-to-output` flag.
- `production_rxn_eqs_*` and `consumption_rxn_eqs_*`: The chemical reaction equation of any production/consumption reactions the compound participates in, specific to the reaction network of a given genome. Added by using the `--add-reactions-to-output` flag.

### Pathway Walk evidence for potentially-exchanged compounds

Each line of this file describes the reaction chain evidence for a compound from _one KEGG Pathway Map_, in _one organism_. In each case, we report the _longest_ reaction chain that we could find (rather than reporting all of the many possible chains). If a compound is present in multiple Pathway Maps, each map gets its own line.

|**`compound`**|**`compound_name`**|**`longest_chain_compound_names`**|**`longest_chain_compounds`**|**`longest_chain_reactions`**|**`longest_reaction_chain_length`**|**`maximum_overlap`**|**`organism`**|**`pathway_map`**|**`proportion_overlap`**|**`type`**|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|cpd00024|2-Oxoglutarate||||None|None|B_cica|00350|None|production|
|cpd00024|2-Oxoglutarate||||None|None|S_muel|00350|None|consumption|
|cpd00065|L-Tryptophan|L-Tryptophan,L-Tryptophanyl-tRNA(Trp)|C00078,C03512|rn:R03664|1|1|B_cica|00970|1.0|consumption|
|cpd00383|Shikimate||||4|None|B_cica|00400|None|production|
|cpd00383|Shikimate|Shikimate,3-phosphoshikimate,5-O--1-Carboxyvinyl-3-phosphoshikimate,Chorismate,Prephenate,Phenylpyruvate,L-Phenylalanine|C00493,C03175,C01269,C00251,C00254,C00166,C00079|rn:R02412,rn:R03460,rn:R01714,rn:R01715,rn:R01373,rn:R00694|6|3|S_muel|00400|0.5|consumption|
|cpd03607|4-(Phosphonooxy)-threonine||||2|None|B_cica|00750|None|production|
|cpd03607|4-(Phosphonooxy)-threonine|4-(Phosphonooxy)-threonine,4-Hydroxy-L-threonine,Pyridoxol,Glycolaldehyde|C06055,C06056,C00314,C00266|rn:R05086,rn:R01913,rn:R05840|3|0|S_muel|00750|None|consumption|

- `compound`: the ModelSEED ID of the potentially-exchanged compound
- `compound_name`: the human-readable name of the compound
- `longest_chain_compound_names`: a comma-separated list of all (human-readable) compound names in this reaction chain
- `longest_chain_compounds`: a comma-separated list of all ModelSEED compound IDs in this reaction chain
- `longest_chain_reactions`: a comma-separated list of all ModelSEED reaction IDs in this reaction chain
- `longest_reaction_chain_length`: the length of (number of reactions in) this reaction chain
- `maximum_overlap`: the largest number of overlapping reactions between this reaction chain and similar chains in the other organism
- `organism`: in which genome was this reaction chain found?
- `pathway_map`: in which KEGG Pathway Map was this reaction chain found?
- `proportion_overlap`: the maximum proportion of reactions that overlap between this reaction chain and similar chains in the other organism
- `type`: whether or not this is a 'production' chain or a 'consumption' chain for the compound

### Unique compounds

Each line of this file describes a metabolite that is found in only one of the organisms' reaction networks.

|**`compound_id`**|**`compound_name`**|**`genomes`**|**`produced_by`**|**`consumed_by`**|**`prediction_method`**|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|cpd00002|ATP|B_cica|B_cica|B_cica|Pathway_Map_Walk|
|cpd00003|NAD|B_cica|B_cica|B_cica|Pathway_Map_Walk|
|cpd00005|NADPH|B_cica|B_cica|None|Pathway_Map_Walk|

It uses the same standard columns and additional columns as the output for potentially-exchanged compounds.

### Compounds with no prediction

This is an optional output file, that is only generated when using the flag `--report-compounds-with-no-prediction`. Each line of this file describes a metabolite that was _not_ predicted to be either potentially-exchanged or unique between the input pair of genomes. Rather, these are compounds that are produced by both organisms and consumed by neither, consumed by both organisms and produced by neither, or produced and consumed by both organisms.

|**`compound_id`**|**`compound_name`**|**`genomes`**|**`produced_by`**|**`consumed_by`**|**`prediction_method`**|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|cpd00227|L-Homoserine|B_cica,S_muel|B_cica,S_muel|B_cica,S_muel|Pathway_Map_Walk|
|cpd19009|alpha-D-Mannose|None|None|None|Pathway_Map_Walk|
|cpd29753|C15811|B_cica,S_muel|None|B_cica,S_muel|Reaction_Network_Subset|
|cpd00190|beta-D-Glucose|B_cica,S_muel|B_cica,S_muel|None|Reaction_Network_Subset|

It uses the same standard columns and some additional columns as the output for potentially-exchanged compounds.
metabolite-exchange-predictions.name: PREDICTED METABOLITE EXCHANGES

equivalent-compounds-txt.source_markdown:
This file describes pairs of ModelSEED compound IDs that should be considered equivalent to each other for the purposes of predicting potential metabolic exchanges with %(anvi-predict-metabolic-exchanges)s.

## Example file

The file should be tab-delimited and have four columns. The first two columns contain the pair of ModelSEED compound IDs that you consider equivalent, and the second two columns contain their respective human-readable names (for convenience when reading the file).

|**`compound_id`**|**`equivalent_id`**|**`name`**|**`equivalent_name`**|
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|cpd00035|cpd01003|L-Alanine|Alanine|
|cpd00039|cpd19182|L-Lysine|Lysine|
|cpd00041|cpd19181|L-Aspartate|Aspartate|

## Pro Tip: generating the file automatically

If you run %(anvi-predict-metabolic-exchanges)s with the `--use-equivalent-amino-acids` flag, it will create a file of this type containing the set of amino acid compound equivalents it automatically finds in the ModelSEED database:

{{ codestart }}
anvi-predict-metabolic-exchanges -c1 %(contigs-db)s -c2 %(contigs-db)s \
                                 -O ANY_PREFIX \
                                 --use-equivalent-amino-acids
{{ codestop }}

You can modify the resulting output file as you want to remove or add new compound equivalents and make a custom set that can be passed to %(anvi-predict-metabolic-exchanges)s with the `--custom-equivalent-compounds-file` parameter.

genome-pairs.source_markdown:
This input file type describes pairs of genomes that go together in an analysis, and is usually paired with an %(external-genomes)s file that describes where the %(contigs-db) associated with each genome name is located.

In the context of %(anvi-predict-metabolic-exchanges)s, this file describes which pairs of genomes to predict exchanges between.

The file should be tab-delimited and contain at least two columns named `genome_1` and `genome_2`. Here is an example:

|**`genome_1`**|**`genome_2`**|
|:--|:--|
|name_of_one_genome|name_of_another_genome|
|E_coli|Pelagibacter_sp|
|another_genome|awesomegenome|

As long as the genome names match to those described in the accompanying %(external-genomes)s file, you should be good to go.

contigs.source_markdown:
This workflow is extremely useful if you have one or more %(fasta)s files that describe one or more contig sequences for your genomes or assembled metagenomes, and all you want to turn them into %(contigs-db)s files.

{:.warning}
If you have not yet run anvi'o programs %(anvi-setup-ncbi-cogs)s and %(anvi-setup-scg-taxonomy)s on your system yet, you will get a cryptic error from this workflow if you run it with the default %(workflow-config)s. You can avoid this by first running these two anvi'o programs to setup the necessary databases (which is done only once for every anvi'o installation), **or** set the rules for COG functions and/or SCG taxonomy to `run=false` explicitly.

To start things going with this workflow, first ask anvi'o to give you a default %(workflow-config)s file for the contigs workflow:

```bash
anvi-run-workflow -w contigs \
                  --get-default-config config-contigs-default.json
```

This will generate a file in your work directory called `config-contigs-default.json`. You should investigate its contents, and familiarize youself with it. It should look something like this, but much longer:
and you could examine its content to find out all possible options to tweak. We included a much simpler config file, `config-contigs.json`, in the mock data package for the sake of demonstrating how the contigs workflow works:

```json
{
    "workflow_name": "contigs",
    "config_version": "2",
    "fasta_txt": "fasta.txt",
    "output_dirs": {
        "FASTA_DIR": "01_FASTA",
        "CONTIGS_DIR": "02_CONTIGS",
        "LOGS_DIR": "00_LOGS"
    }
}
```

The only mandatory thing you need to do is to (1) manually create a %(fasta-txt)s file to describe the name and location of each FASTA file you wish to work with, and (2) make sure the `fasta_txt` variable in your %(workflow-config)s point to the location of your %(fasta-txt)s.

To see if everything looks alright, you can simply run the following command, which should generate a 'workflow graph' for you, given your config file parameters and input files:

```bash
anvi-run-workflow -w contigs \
                  -c config-contigs.json \
                  --save-workflow-graph
```

For the example config file shown above, this command will generate something similar to this:

[![DAG-contigs](../../images/workflows/contigs/DAG-contigs.png)]( ../../images/workflows/contigs/DAG-contigs.png){:.center-img .width-50}

{:.notice}
Please note that the generation of this workflow graph requires the usage of a program called [dot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOT_(graph_description_language)). If you are using MAC OSX, you can use [dot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOT_(graph_description_language)) by installing [graphviz](http://www.graphviz.org/) through `brew` or `conda`.

If everything looks alright, you can run this workflow the following way:

```bash
anvi-run-workflow -w contigs \
                  -c config-contigs.json
```

If everything goes smoothly, you should see happy messages flowing on your screen, and at the end of it all you should see your contigs databases are generated and annotated properly. At the end of this process, you will have all your %(contigs-db)s files in the `02_CONTIGS` directory (as per the instructions in the config file, which you can change). You can use the program %(anvi-display-contigs-stats)s on one of them to see if everything makes sense.

Workflow logs will be under `00_LOGS/contigs` by default. Rule logs are organized by rule name, and the contigs workflow writes a tab-delimited manifest at `00_LOGS/contigs/contigs-workflow-manifest.tsv` that points to each job's log and records whether it succeeded or failed.

## Predicting protein structures

The contigs workflow can also predict the structures of the genes in each %(contigs-db)s, and store them in a %(structure-db)s using %(anvi-gen-structure-database)s. This step is off by default. To turn it on, set `run` to `true` for the rule `anvi_gen_structure_database` in your %(workflow-config)s. Every parameter of the prediction (including the `--engine`, which can be `modeller` or `colabfold`) lives under this rule:

```json
"anvi_gen_structure_database": {
    "run": true,
    "threads": 4,
    "--engine": "colabfold",
    "--colabfold-conda-env": "colabfold",
    "--colabfold-db": "/path/to/colabfold_db"
}
```

The workflow writes one %(structure-db)s per FASTA file into `03_STRUCTURE`, e.g., `03_STRUCTURE/SAMPLE_01-STRUCTURE.db`. The prediction does not hold up the rest of the workflow: it only needs the %(contigs-db)s, and annotating the %(contigs-db)s afterwards will not trigger a new prediction.

Once a %(structure-db)s exists, the workflow never touches it again, even if you change the structure parameters in your %(workflow-config)s or the genes of interest of that %(contigs-db)s: predicting structures can take days, and the workflow will not delete them. Anvi'o lists these %(structure-db)s files every time you run the workflow. To predict the structures of a %(contigs-db)s again, move or remove its %(structure-db)s first. To only add genes to it, you can use %(anvi-update-structure-database)s. The workflow writes each %(structure-db)s under a temporary name (e.g., `03_STRUCTURE/SAMPLE_01-STRUCTURE-INCOMPLETE.db`) and only renames it once it is complete, so a job that failed or was killed (for instance, by your cluster's time limit) does not leave behind an unfinished %(structure-db)s under its final name. If you stop the workflow yourself with Ctrl-C, please check `03_STRUCTURE` before running it again.

The workflow also makes sure each existing %(structure-db)s was made from the %(contigs-db)s it belongs to, and stops if it was not (for instance, if you made a %(contigs-db)s again), so you can move or remove the old %(structure-db)s.

With MODELLER, a %(structure-db)s may contain no structures at all, when MODELLER does not find a good enough template for any of the genes of interest. This is not an error: the %(structure-db)s still records the genes anvi'o tried.

### Choosing genes

By default, anvi'o predicts a structure for every gene of every %(contigs-db)s, and warns you when it is about to do so. A single genome has thousands of genes, so this can take a very long time. To limit the prediction to some genes, add a `structure_genes_of_interest` column to your %(fasta-txt)s that points to a %(genes-of-interest-txt)s for each FASTA file:

|name|path|structure_genes_of_interest|
|:--|:--|:--|
|SAMPLE_01|path/to/sample_01.fa|genes_01.txt|
|SAMPLE_02|path/to/sample_02.fa||

Here, anvi'o predicts structures for the genes listed in `genes_01.txt` for `SAMPLE_01`, and for every gene of `SAMPLE_02`.

Since gene caller ids only exist once a %(contigs-db)s is built, you can first run the workflow without structure prediction, pick your genes, add the column to your %(fasta-txt)s, turn on `anvi_gen_structure_database`, and then run the workflow again: anvi'o will only run the missing structure steps.

### Splitting ColabFold into CPU and GPU steps

ColabFold generates multiple sequence alignments (MSA) on the CPU, then predicts structures on the GPU. With a local ColabFold database (`--colabfold-db`), you can set `split_msa_and_predict` to `true` for `anvi_gen_structure_database` to run these as two separate jobs: `colabfold_msa` (with `--only-msa`) and `colabfold_predict` (with `--only-predict`). This way, a cluster can run each one on the appropriate node. Each of these two rules has its own `threads`, and takes every other parameter from `anvi_gen_structure_database`. The MSAs go into a temporary `03_STRUCTURE/SAMPLE_01-COLABFOLD-MSA` directory that the workflow removes once the %(structure-db)s is built.

### GPU resources

The rules that predict structures with ColabFold (`colabfold_predict`, and `anvi_gen_structure_database` when `--engine` is `colabfold`) declare a GPU through the snakemake resource `gpu=1`. MODELLER and `colabfold_msa` declare `gpu=0`. You can change this number with the `gpu` parameter of `anvi_gen_structure_database` and `colabfold_predict`.

It is up to you to map this resource onto your scheduler.
